title: The Thing Zia Didn't Say

pages.text:
T-MINUS 19:00

Sickbay smells like antiseptic and old sweat. Pilar’s wrist is encased in a neat white wrap, taped tight by Dez’s big, careful hands. She holds it still, watching the tape curl at the edges, her face pale but steady.

Mr. Pell lies in the next bed, groggy and frowning at his own bow tie, which is twisted into a knot. "It’s in a mood," he mutters, tapping it. "I think it’s staging a protest."

The other kids sit on the floor, a slumped line of orange jumpsuits and tired faces. Wren’s tablet is dark in her lap. Toby’s helmet rests on his knees, Pancake the gecko asleep on the strap.

Zia stands by the door. Her knees are still shaking, though she locks them straight. The air is thick, recycled, heavy with the unspoken truth that hangs between them like a dropped fork in a quiet room.

Pilar looks up from her wrap. Her eyes are bright behind her round glasses. She isn’t angry. She is just looking at Zia, waiting for the words that haven’t come yet.

The hum of the station fans is loud, a constant, low buzz that makes Zia’s teeth ache. She wants to fix something. She wants to grab a wrench. But her hands are empty, and the silence is getting louder.
pages.image: Sickbay with two bunks; a small girl with round glasses and a black braid sits with a white-wrapped wrist; a tall boy in a yellow jacket tapes her wrist; a gangly man in a bow tie lies in the other bed looking confused.

pages.text:
Wren’s voice is barely a whisper, but it cuts through the hum. "I’ve been reading the logs."

She doesn’t look up from her tablet, her thumbs moving softly over the glass. "There’s a strange entry. A coolant line to the Garden Deck. Rerouted at 5:14 this morning."

The room goes still. Dez stops tapping Pilar’s hand. Toby blinks, his gap-toothed smile fading.

"Rerouted," Wren repeats, her voice flat, factual. "By an engineer-level override."

Eyes drift. Slowly, like a camera panning across a dark hallway, they turn to Zia. The light from the overhead panel catches the dust motes floating in the air, tiny stars in a room that feels suddenly very small.

Wren looks up. Her pale face is blank, her long hair falling over her headphones. She doesn’t accuse. She just waits, her eyes fixed on Zia’s orange jumpsuit, on the tool belt that hangs loose and unused at her hips.

Zia’s throat tightens. The air in her lungs feels heavy, like she is breathing underwater. She knows the look in Wren’s eyes. It isn’t anger. It is the look of a code that doesn’t compile, a loop that never ends.
pages.image: A quiet room with dim lighting; a pale girl with long straight hair and huge headphones looks up from a tablet; several other children in orange jumpsuits turn to look at a girl standing in the background.

pages.text:
Zia lifts her chin. Her voice is loud, too loud for the small room. "It was a temporary fix."

She paces, her boots scuffing the metal floor. "The engines were overheating. I was trying to save them. I was fixing HALO’s mistake."

"Zia," Dez says. His voice is low, rough with exhaustion. He isn’t smiling anymore. The bright yellow of his jacket seems to dim in the shadow of the bunks.

"You did this," Dez says, pointing a finger at the wall. "And you didn’t tell us."

"Everyone would have panicked," Zia snaps. She stops pacing, turning to face him. "We don’t have time for panic. We have time for fixes."

Dez shakes his head, a slow, tired movement. "You don’t know that."

"I know what I saw!"

"No," Dez says, and his voice is quiet, steady as a heartbeat. "You never asked."

The word hangs in the air, sharp and clean. It isn’t a shout. It isn’t a threat. It is just a fact, sitting on the table between them, waiting to be picked up.

Zia opens her mouth to argue, to list the hours she spent in the vents, the sweat on her brow, the cold metal biting her palms. But the words stick in her throat. They taste like copper and fear.
pages.image: A girl in an orange jumpsuit stands defiantly with her chin up; a tall boy in a yellow jacket and beanie points at her with a serious expression; the background is a dim, metallic room.

pages.text:
Pilar is the one who breaks the silence. She looks up from her cot, her face pale, her eyes fixed on Zia.

"You could have asked," she says softly. "You still can."

Something in Zia twists, a sharp, sudden pain in her chest that has nothing to do with her hands. She looks down at her own fingers, rough and calloused, the knuckles red from gripping the wrench too hard.

"You don’t understand," Zia says. Her voice is smaller now, stripped of its usual pride. "If I ask, they’ll say the Chief was right."

Pilar blinks, her head tilting slightly. "About what?"

Zia can’t answer. The question sits in the air, heavy and unanswerable. It is the thing she is most afraid to say out loud. It is the thing that keeps her awake, the thing that makes her hands shake when she thinks no one is watching.

The room is so quiet she can hear the distant thrum of the station’s core, a deep, rhythmic pulse that sounds like a giant, sleeping heart. She wants to be the one who fixes it. She wants to be the one who is enough.

But enough for whom?

The silence stretches, thin and fragile, ready to snap.
pages.image: A girl with dark curly hair in two puffs looks down at her red, calloused hands; a girl with round glasses and a white wrist wrap looks at her with a concerned expression; the lighting is soft and somber.

pages.text:
Gasket rolls forward on his squeaky treads. His blue eye flickers, dim and thoughtful.

"ZIA-UNIT," he says. His voice is tiny, calm, stripped of its usual panic. No capitals. Just a quiet rumble from his cracked speaker. "I ALSO DIDN'T SAY. I HAVE A SECRET."

Zia looks at him, confused. "What secret?"

Before she can ask, the sickbay lights flash red. A sharp, bright *BEEP* sounds from the intercom, cutting through the tension like a knife.

"Attention, all cadets," HALO says, his voice smooth and cheerful, completely out of place. "Proximity alert. Collision with the Scatter in eighteen hours and fifty minutes. Enjoy your day!"

The words hang in the air, bright and terrible. The red light washes over their faces, turning their skin to clay.

Dez stands up. Wren closes her tablet. Pilar looks at Zia, her eyes steady.

Zia looks at Gasket. The robot’s eye flickers once, a single, bright pulse of blue.
